claim: Let \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) and \(y=(y_1,y_2,y_3)\) be positive integer abundance profiles having the same census \(N\), with species labels disregarded. For each integer sample depth \(1\le m\le N\), let \(R_m(x)=3-\binom{N}{m}^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^3\binom{N-x_i}{m}\) denote the exact expected richness after drawing uniformly without replacement. Then, as the integer sample size \(m\) increases from \(2\) through \(N-1\), the nonzero signs of \(R_m(x)-R_m(y)\) change at most once. In particular, if both \(R_2(x)-R_2(y)\) and \(R_{N-1}(x)-R_{N-1}(y)\) are nonzero and have the same sign, then that sign is never reversed at any intermediate depth; if the endpoint signs are opposite, exactly one change of strict ordering occurs. The endpoint quantities are \(R_2=2-\sum_i x_i(x_i-1)/(N(N-1))\) and \(R_{N-1}=3-f_1/N\), where \(f_1\) is the singleton count. The proof reduces the difference of hypergeometric absence numerators to a single-sign-changing integrated abundance-frequency difference weighted by a reverse-monotone-likelihood-ratio binomial kernel. The one-crossing bound is attained: at \(N=10\), the profiles \((6,2,2)\) and \((5,4,1)\) satisfy \(R_3(6,2,2)<R_3(5,4,1)\) but \(R_4(6,2,2)>R_4(5,4,1)\). The conclusion concerns expected rarefaction at integer sample sizes, not arbitrary interpolants or sample-to-sample realizations.
integrity: The infinite-size theorem is proved using discrete convex majorization, double summation by parts and a reverse-monotone-likelihood-ratio binomial kernel. Exact standard-library checks independently enumerate all triples through census 35 and verify the summation and kernel inequalities over large finite domains; the finite checks are not the infinite proof.
scientific_limitations: The statement is for three positive-abundance species, fixed total census, integer-depth hypergeometric rarefaction without replacement, and expected rather than sampled richness. It does not cover arbitrary continuous curve interpolants, more species, extrapolation or sampling uncertainty.
title: A single-crossing law for three-species individual-based rarefaction
